key_facts: **Erythema multiforme (EM)** is an acute immune reaction with **target lesions** (three zones), mostly triggered by **herpes simplex**.
Acral (hands, feet, elbows, knees), symmetrical, appears over 24–72 hours; EM major also involves mucosa.
Not part of the SJS/TEN spectrum: SJS has atypical flat targets, widespread blistering and is usually drug-induced.
Supportive care; treat HSV; recurrent HSV-associated EM may need antiviral prophylaxis (specialist).
Urgent same-day care if mucosal involvement impairs eating, eyes are affected or skin is blistering.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Erythema multiforme (EM)** is an acute, immune-mediated mucocutaneous reaction characterised by **typical target (iris / bull’s-eye) lesions**. Most cases are infection-triggered, especially **HSV**. **EM minor** = skin only; **EM major** = skin plus ≥1 mucosal surface (oral, ocular, genital) — still usually infection-related, and is **not** the same disease as drug-induced SJS/TEN (which has different morphology, drug trigger, and severity).

sub: Young adults 20–40; recurs in some with recurrent HSV.

ul: Predominantly a **type IV (cell-mediated / delayed)** hypersensitivity reaction.
**HSV-1/2** is the leading association (often 1–3 weeks after herpes labialis/genitalis; recurrent EM with recurrent HSV).
Other infections: *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* (esp. children/young adults with respiratory prodrome), less often other viruses/bacteria.
Drugs can rarely trigger EM-like eruptions, but severe drug blistering disease should be managed as SJS/TEN pathway until proven otherwise.
Circulating immune response to microbial antigen → cytotoxic T-cell attack on keratinocytes → epidermal necrosis in the target centre.
HSV (most), *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* (especially children), other infections; drugs less often.
**"EM is mild SJS"**: they are different diseases with different causes and outlooks.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: EM is a **T-cell reaction to viral DNA** deposited in the skin.

mech.t: Fragments of HSV DNA are carried to distant skin by blood cells.
HSV-specific T cells release interferon-γ, damaging keratinocytes.
Dusky or blistered centre (necrosis), pale oedematous ring, red outer ring.
mech.caption: The three zones of a typical target lesion.

mech.t: Lesions favour the hands, feet and extensor limbs.
mech.caption: Acral target lesions on the hands.

histo: Interface dermatitis with necrotic keratinocytes; HSV PCR from a cold sore may help.

head: Feature
Detail
rows: Three zones: dusky/purpuric or blistered centre → pale oedematous ring → outer erythematous ring
Symmetrical; acral preference — hands/feet dorsa, extensor limbs, then trunk; face possible
Oral erosions/ulcers common in EM major; lips crusted; eyes/genitals less often
Mild fever/malaise optional; history of recent cold sore is a strong clue
Lesions appear over days; resolve over 1–4 weeks; may recur with HSV

blocks.h: Why EM belongs in a palmar/plantar week

blocks: EM has an **acral predilection** — it typically begins on the **dorsal hands and feet**, palms, soles and extensor forearms, then spreads centripetally to limbs and (less) trunk. Palm/sole **typical target lesions** are often the clinching sign.

ul: **Typical target:** ≤ 3 cm, round, **three zones** — dark-red/dusky (sometimes blistered or crusted) centre → paler oedematous ring → outer red ring with a sharp edge.
**Raised atypical target:** two zones, palpable — still EM.
**Flat atypical targets / purpuric macules, widespread on trunk** → think **SJS/TEN** (drug-related), especially with mucosal erosions or skin pain.
Palms: thick stratum corneum can make targets look flatter and more "bruise-like"; the iris pattern is often easiest to see here.

ol: **Diagnosis:** erythema multiforme **minor** (typical acral targets, polymorphous papules, **no mucosal involvement**).

**Trigger:** most likely the **preceding viral infection** ("flu" 2 weeks earlier) — EM usually follows infection by 1–3 weeks; **HSV** is the commonest overall trigger (ask about cold sores, even subclinical) and *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* in young adults with respiratory symptoms. Drugs (sulfonamides, antiepileptics, NSAIDs, antibiotics) account for a minority of true EM; **paracetamol** and **chlorphenamine** are rare/doubtful culprits — note them, but the timing and morphology favour infection.

**Treatment:** self-limiting over ~2–4 weeks. Supportive: emollient, moderate–potent topical steroid for symptomatic lesions, oral non-sedating antihistamine for itch/burning, analgesia. Treat identified infection (e.g. aciclovir only if active HSV; macrolide if *Mycoplasma* confirmed). Stop non-essential new drugs. **Recurrent** HSV-associated EM → dermatology may use continuous oral aciclovir/valaciclovir prophylaxis. Systemic steroids only under specialist advice in severe mucosal EM.

**Safety-net / urgent referral:** mucosal (oral, eye, genital) erosions, blistering/skin detachment, skin pain, fever/systemic upset, widespread flat atypical targets → same-day assessment for EM major vs SJS/TEN; eye involvement → ophthalmology.

variants.name: Mucosal (EM major)
variants.t: Crusted lips, oral erosions. *Site: Lips, mouth.*

sub: Mycoplasma-induced rash and mucositis (MIRM) causes severe mucositis with few skin lesions.

ul: **Clinical** in classic post-HSV target pattern.
History: recent HSV, *Mycoplasma*/respiratory symptoms, drugs, mucosal symptoms, eye symptoms.
Exam: full skin + oral + eyes + genitals.
Investigate if atypical / severe: *Mycoplasma* testing if respiratory; HSV swabs of cold sores; consider biopsy if uncertain.
**Do not** label as SJS solely because mucosa is involved — target morphology + infection trigger favour EM.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses

ddx.name: SJS / TEN
ddx.f: Flat atypical targets, widespread purpuric macules, sheet-like detachment; **drugs**; very unwell.

ddx.name: Urticaria / urticaria multiforme
ddx.f: Migratory wheals < 24 h; no fixed dusky centre.

ddx.name: Fixed drug eruption
ddx.f: Round dusky plaque recurring at the same site.

blocks: Also consider: *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*-induced rash and mucositis (RIME), Kawasaki disease, toxic shock syndrome, acute GVHD, linear IgA bullous dermatosis (vancomycin), acute cutaneous lupus (TEN-like), paraneoplastic pemphigus.

ul: Emollients; bland oral care (soft diet, antiseptic/analgesic mouth rinses per local advice) for oral EM.
Analgesia; rest; treat concurrent HSV cold sore if active (topical/oral antivirals per licence/BNF).
Document drug history; stop any newly started suspect drug pending specialist advice if morphology atypical.
Mild cutaneous EM: often supportive only in primary care.
Recurrent HSV-associated EM: dermatology may consider continuous or intermittent **oral antiviral prophylaxis** (e.g. aciclovir — specialist/experienced initiation).
**Urgent same-day / emergency** if: extensive mucosal disease impairing intake, ocular involvement, suspected SJS/TEN, systemic toxicity, inability to distinguish from severe drug reaction.
Ophthalmology review for eye involvement.
IP: do **not** start systemic steroids for presumed EM without specialist advice (may be used in selected severe cases under derm).

ladder.t: Emollients; soft diet and antiseptic / analgesic mouth rinses for oral EM; analgesia; rest. Document drug history; stop a newly started suspect drug pending advice if morphology atypical.
**Potent topical steroid** to itchy / inflamed skin lesions. Treat an active cold sore (topical / oral antiviral per BNF).
**Continuous or intermittent oral antiviral prophylaxis** (e.g. aciclovir): specialist / experienced initiation.
Systemic steroids only in selected severe cases under dermatology.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Systemic steroids**: Don’t start for presumed EM without specialist advice.

refer.t: Mucosal erosions with **skin pain, blistering or skin loss**: possible **SJS / TEN**; stop suspect drugs, admit same day.
Unable to eat or drink: admission for fluids and analgesia.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Mucosal erosions (mouth, eyes, genitals) with skin pain, blistering or skin loss: possible **SJS/TEN**, so stop suspect drugs and admit the same day.
Eye involvement: same-day ophthalmology.
Unable to eat or drink: admission for fluids and analgesia.
Eye scarring in EM major; dehydration from painful mouth.
Resolves in 2–4 weeks without scarring; recurrences common with HSV.

pearls: Teach patients with recurrent cold sores that EM can follow HSV — early antiviral for prodromal HSV may reduce triggers (individualise).
Emphasise difference between EM major and SJS — reduces panic but does not delay referral when severe.
Warn that scars are uncommon but pigment change can linger.
Pregnancy: check BNF for any antivirals/steroids contemplated.
